The following members of the National Advisory Council on Poverty contributed to the preparation of this year’s report:
Marie Christian, Member with particular responsibilities for children’s issues
The Council would like to thank former members whose work has been foundational in promoting poverty reduction in Canada.
The Council also expresses its gratitude to government officials who assisted in the work this year and in previous years. These include members of the Council’s Secretariat in the Social Policy Directorate at Employment and Social Development Canada, as well as public servants from Statistics Canada and other key federal government departments. Their ongoing support makes it possible for the Council to fulfill its mandate.
The National Advisory Council on Poverty dedicates this 2026 progress report to all the individuals who selflessly shared their stories of success and struggles. Your invaluable insights are the foundation on which Canada builds better systems, enhances support and improves the lives of others experiencing poverty or at risk of experiencing it. You are the beating heart of this report.
The Council also extends its heartfelt gratitude to the Tamarack Institute and Campaign 2000 for their support in coordinating regional roundtables as well as the local organizations that welcomed the Council during visits to Edmonton (AB), Montreal (QC), Toronto (ON) and Vancouver (BC). These organizations (see Annex A) were instrumental in connecting Council members with individuals who experience poverty, enabling a better understanding of how poverty is experienced in their regions. The Council also recognizes the significant strain these organizations are under and acknowledges that those working in this sector are continually being asked to do more with fewer resources. Thank you!
On behalf of the National Advisory Council on Poverty, I am pleased to present our 2026 report on the progress of Opportunity for All—Canada’s First Poverty Reduction Strategy .
Recent data shows that progress toward reducing poverty in Canada remains slow. In 2024, 4.5 million people, 11.0% of Canadians, continued to live in poverty, with little improvement from the previous year. While progress is possible, it will require focused effort, sustained investment, and courageous policy choices.
The Council consistently hears that affordability has become the defining challenge of our time. Rising costs for housing, food and transportation are outpacing wages, benefits and supports, leaving many people, whether working or not, trapped in survival mode.
Poverty isn’t experienced equally. This year we heard from members of Black, Urban Indigenous, and 2SLGBTQIA+ communities who face disproportionate barriers rooted in systemic racism, colonialism and exclusion. Across the stories people shared with us, a consistent message emerged: poverty goes beyond financial hardship. It also reflects inequities in how systems serve people.
Poverty is deeply structural. Systems intended to provide support are often fragmented, difficult to navigate and reactive rather than preventative. In this context, poverty is not only about low incomes; it’s also about a lack of access to opportunity, stability and dignity.
As we met with people across the country, we witnessed strong community connections, compassionate care and bold, sustainable solutions. To reach Canada’s 2030 target of reducing poverty by 50% relative to 2015 rates, we must build on these strengths by advancing affordability, ensuring income adequacy and prioritizing equity and justice. This means addressing the rising cost of essentials, strengthening and simplifying the systems people rely on and designing policies that work for those most affected by poverty. Taken together, these aren’t abstract goals. They are concrete actions that would reduce poverty.
Poverty in Canada is not inevitable. Through deliberate choices to improve affordability, strengthen support systems and confront inequities, poverty can be prevented.
Poverty is a collective choice, and we can choose a different future. Let’s choose a stronger, more inclusive Canada where everyone can be themselves, belong and thrive.
Chairperson, National Advisory Council on Poverty
Canada has made progress in reducing poverty since 2015, but the rapid improvements seen during the early pandemic years haven’t continued and recent progress has stalled. In 2024, about 4.5 million people in Canada, or 11.0% of the population, were living with poverty. This is a 26% drop compared to 2015 levels, but this remains short of the legislated target of a 50% reduction by 2030. With only a few years left to meet this target, the Government of Canada must take urgent action to close the gap.
Recent trends indicate that poverty reduction has been inconsistent. Temporary supports during the pandemic caused a sharp decline in poverty rates in 2020, but many of those gains were lost as those measures ended. While the poverty rate stabilized between 2023 and 2024, progress has largely plateaued, raising concerns about Canada’s ability to meet its poverty reduction goals.
Income-based measures, such as the Market Basket Measure, are important for tracking poverty but don’t fully reflect lived experiences of poverty. Different indicators measure aspects of poverty, such as homelessness, food insecurity and social exclusion. Some of these indicators have worsened despite the decline in poverty rates. In addition, many factors shape the experience of poverty, including rising costs, systemic barriers to support and unequal access to services and opportunities.
Poverty is unevenly distributed. Some population groups, including racialized individuals, Indigenous people living off reserve, people with disabilities and lone-parent families, face significantly higher poverty rates. These disparities reflect ongoing systemic inequities that existing data may not fully capture. People facing multiple forms of discrimination, such as those based on race, gender, or disability, are often at greater risk of experiencing deeper and longer-term poverty.
The National Advisory Council on Poverty reports annually on the progress made toward Canada’s poverty reduction target to reduce poverty by 50% by 2030, relative to 2015 levels. The report also contains insights gathered through the Council’s ongoing dialogue on poverty with individuals and organizations engaged across the country.
This year, the Council aimed to gain a deeper understanding of the factors that keep some population groups in poverty and to identify policy actions to help reduce or eliminate poverty within these groups. As such, besides examining how people are experiencing poverty in general, the Council also focused on gaining a better understanding of how poverty affects specific populations differently.
To support its examination, the Council focused its engagement on 3 key population groups: members of Black communities, Indigenous people living in urban areas (Urban Indigenous people), and 2SLGBTQIA+ individuals. The Council chose to focus on these groups because they experience high rates of poverty and face significant discrimination that keeps them in poverty.
From November 2025 to January 2026, the Council held 32 conversations involving over 380 individuals with lived or living experience of poverty and 4 regional roundtables attended by over 120 community leaders and changemakers.
The data and lived experiences gathered indicate that, while overall poverty has stabilized, inequities are growing and the depth of poverty is increasing for many. This puts Canada’s poverty reduction goals at risk. This report outlines the progress in reducing poverty in Canada and shares insights from the Council’s focused work on advancing equity to end poverty.
The costs of poverty in Canada are significant and far-reaching. Beyond its impact on individuals, poverty strains public systems like health care and the criminal justice system, while limiting economic participation. Many people pointed out that reactive, crisis-driven responses are costly and ineffective. Instead, investments that address root causes and focus on prevention can improve well-being and support stronger, more inclusive economic outcomes.
At a human level, poverty can feel dehumanizing. Many described support systems as rigid, punitive, and hard to navigate, causing additional stress and discouraging people from seeking help. Poverty also has wider societal effects. Stigma, racism and discrimination create exclusion and erode social cohesion, deepening divisions within communities. These negative dynamics stem from current gaps in systems and long-standing inequities, including the ongoing impacts of colonialism and systemic discrimination, which affect access to opportunities and resources.
Addressing poverty adequately requires a commitment to advancing equity and justice. This means shifting from broad approaches to solutions that tackle causes, remove systemic barriers, and consider the realities of those most affected. Without this shift, poverty reduction efforts will continue to fall short of reaching those who need support the most.
This year’s discussions highlighted how people experience poverty within interconnected systems in Canada. While experiences differed among population groups, consistent themes emerged: systems are fragmented, hard to navigate, and often fail to meet people’s needs. Many participants noted that support services do not consider their circumstances and can even cause harm or re-traumatization. Experiences of racism, colonialism and discrimination—alongside bias related to gender identity, sexual orientation, and income—continue to shape how the system treats individuals.
Income insecurity is a widespread concern. Participants from all 3 groups shared struggles to cover basic needs, as wages and benefits don’t keep up with living costs. Many reported living in survival mode, constantly choosing between essentials like housing, food, and transportation, with little ability to plan.
Housing challenges were a major issue for Black, Urban Indigenous, and 2SLGBTQIA+ participants, who faced barriers such as discrimination, affordability issues, and a lack of safe options. For some, especially 2SLGBTQIA+ individuals, housing instability was closely tied to family rejection and lack of support.
Barriers extend across other systems. Newcomers described difficulties with immigration processes, credential recognition, and finding jobs, often facing racism and exclusion. Participants pointed out inequities in health care, education, child welfare, and the criminal justice system, where systemic biases lead to poorer outcomes and perpetuate cycles of disadvantage. These examples of lived experiences demonstrate that current systems aren’t adequately meeting people’s needs and often reinforce the barriers that contribute to poverty.
Meeting Canada’s poverty reduction target requires urgent and coordinated action across all sectors of society. Despite long-standing commitments—including the legislated goal of reducing poverty by 50% by 2030 and adherence to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals—progress has slowed, and many people still can’t meet their basic needs.
Reducing and ending poverty is a shared responsibility, requiring a whole-of-society approach. While the federal government plays a key leadership role in setting direction and ensuring accountability, provinces and territories are responsible for delivering essential services like social assistance, health care, and education. Non-profit organizations provide critical front-line support, and employers play a vital role in creating inclusive job markets and providing fair wages. Improved coordination and accountability across these actors are essential for making meaningful and lasting progress.
With the 2030 deadline fast approaching, the Council stresses that meeting Canada’s poverty reduction target will require bold and deliberate action focused on equity. This includes efforts to address systemic and structural barriers that disproportionately affect some groups. Ending poverty in Canada is achievable, but it requires sustained political will, meaningful collaboration, and a clear commitment to investing in people.
Based on its engagement with individuals, service providers, community organizations, and change makers, the Council has developed the following recommendations. It also drew on its analysis of available data and systems. These recommendations aim to enhance accountability and collaboration. They also seek to advance equity and justice within systems. Also, they focus on improving income supports and addressing affordability, particularly in housing. Finally, the recommendations also point to the importance of better supporting communities and the non-profit sector.
According to Opportunity for All—Canada’s First Poverty Reduction Strategy (the Poverty Reduction Strategy), “Every Canadian deserves a real and fair chance to succeed, no matter where they live or where they come from.” (Employment and Social Development Canada, 2018) The Poverty Reduction Strategy emphasizes that achieving lasting progress toward a poverty-free Canada is a shared responsibility that relies on strong partnerships, collaboration, and ongoing accountability among all levels of government, communities, organizations, and individuals. While the federal government can act on its own, meaningful results require leadership in collaboration with others.
To this end, the Council recommends that the Government of Canada:
Position poverty reduction as a core national investment priority. This could be done by:
requiring that all major Budget proposals and fiscal commitments be assessed against their expected contribution to poverty reduction. This exercise could mirror or complement frameworks such as the Gender-based Analysis Plus (GBA+) and Quality of Life Framework for Canada
integrating poverty reduction metrics into Departmental Results Frameworks or program performance reporting and evaluation
embedding an accountability framework in federal funding transfers to ensure provinces and territories use the funding to enhance and supplement current benefits and programs, not replace them
Based on the most recent poverty data and input received this year, the Council is confident that existing poverty reduction measures won’t be sufficient to meet the target set out in the Poverty Reduction Strategy. Poverty rates remain high and disproportionately affect groups made most marginal. This highlights the ineffectiveness of a one-size-fits-all approach to poverty reduction. Efforts focused on improving affordability haven’t adequately addressed the real challenges faced by people living with poverty, particularly those made most marginal, and have often left many people further behind.
Over the years, the Council has heard that systems are not only difficult to navigate, they are also rooted in discrimination, colonialism, and racism. For groups like Black, Urban Indigenous, and 2SLGBTQIA+ communities, these systems often fail to reflect their lived realities. Addressing the effects of colonialism, racism and discrimination requires an ongoing commitment to equity, equality, justice and inclusion. Ensuring that poverty reduction efforts address systemic barriers will help advance equitable outcomes for groups made most marginal and strengthen society overall.
To this end, we recommend that the Government of Canada:
Adopt a structured and collaborative approach with provinces and territories to embed equity-based objectives at the outset of new and renewed federal funding transfers (for example, social, health, and immigration). This could include:
developing a common understanding of equity priorities
identifying target populations to be prioritized
Support the development, adoption and implementation of distinction-based poverty reduction plans for specific population groups. The groups with the greatest burden of poverty should be prioritized with the goal of reducing their poverty rates to meet or fall below the national average. Additionally, these plans should:
acknowledge and address the diverse experiences of poverty within population groups, including barriers related to income, employment, housing, education, health, child welfare, immigration, and access to services
be co-developed with members of these population groups, ensuring their diverse experiences, needs and perspectives shape policy and program design, implementation and evaluation
be grounded in disaggregated, community-informed and interpreted data, supported by improved availability and ethical, culturally appropriate collection methods that respect privacy, minimize harm, and are led in partnership with members of the populations
enhance federal strategies or initiatives by applying a poverty lens to, for example, Canada’s Anti-Racism Strategy (2024–2028) and the Federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan
Direct income supports for individuals are effective ways to reduce poverty. For instance, the Canada Child Benefit has and continues to provide significant financial support for families, regardless of whether the parents are working or receiving social assistance. As well, although the federal government didn’t design the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB) as a poverty reduction measure, it provided financial supports to many individuals during the pandemic and reduced poverty rates significantly during that period. While CERB was temporary and didn’t reach all individuals, such as those receiving social assistance or earning less than $5,000 in employment income, its implementation offers useful insights for the design of a basic income. The CERB acted as a form of basic income for eligible applicants, temporarily improving many individuals’ financial situations.
Not all direct income transfers are effective, though. Social assistance rates often leave individuals well below the poverty line, and the rules governing these benefits don’t provide a clear path out of poverty. Many low-wage workers are exhausted, frustrated, and still unable to afford necessities, forcing them to choose between essentials like rent, heat, food, or transportation.
Additionally, the private sector has a role to play in poverty reduction. The fact that corporations are reporting record profits while many individuals struggle indicates the need for employers to pay a living wage or contribute more through taxation to support those in need.
Establishing an income floor is a viable path to reaching the 2030 poverty reduction target and ultimately eradicating poverty. It would also enhance individuals’ financial stability, enabling them to meet their needs with dignity.
To this end, we recommend that the Government of Canada:
Establish regional income floors, in partnership with provinces, territories and Indigenous governments, to ensure everyone reaches at least Canada’s Official Poverty Line through wages, government income supports, or a combination of both. Additionally, while increasing incomes, the federal government should also identify and implement measures to slow the rising cost of essentials (for example, food, clothing, transportation, shelter, and communication services). Measures should consider regional economic conditions and realities to ensure that inflation doesn’t offset or erode income gains.
Leverage existing and introduce new federal programs and funding transfers to expand access to supported employment pathways for people facing systemic barriers. Populations disproportionately impacted by poverty due to labour market exclusion should be prioritized. This includes Black people, Urban Indigenous people, 2SLGBTQIA+ people, newcomers, people with disabilities, and youth. Efforts could include:
increasing funding to support flexible child care with expanded services for non-standard and shift-based work hours
requiring, in funding agreements, that employers adopt and implement anti-racism and anti-discrimination policies to promote accountability and support inclusive hiring and employment practices
accelerating and streamlining foreign credential recognition
further investing in targeted work readiness and skills training initiatives to in-demand sectors for youth, immigrants, and other groups facing heightened barriers to employment
Participants representing population groups engaged this year reported significant barriers to affordability. They stressed that incomes, whether from social assistance, federal benefits, employment, or a combination of these, aren’t keeping pace with the rising cost of living. This gap forces many people into survival mode, leading to a host of issues that affect both physical and mental health, safety, and interactions with the criminal justice system. However, the Council acknowledges that simply raising incomes may not solve these affordability challenges, as higher cash transfers could contribute to inflation if the cost of essential goods continues to rise.
Given these ongoing affordability issues, the Council reiterates its 2025 recommendation for the Government of Canada to “look for ways to slow the rising cost of essentials, like food, transportation, clothing and other necessities, so that inflation doesn’t offset or cancel income gains.” (National Advisory Council on Poverty, 2025)
Most importantly, the Council urges the federal government to prioritize the availability, affordability, and adequacy of housing for people living in poverty or near the poverty line. Many individuals reported spending nearly all their income on rent and utilities. As a fixed household expense, housing is a significant source of financial stress. High housing and related costs push people into poverty or keep them there. Ensuring affordable and adequate housing is available is essential for helping individuals achieve financial stability and spending power.
To this end, we recommend that the Government of Canada:
Commit to expanding non-market housing, recognizing its essential role in preventing and reducing homelessness, so it makes up a much larger share of Canada’s housing stock, from 3.5% to at least 7.1%, in line with the OECD average, through sustained and targeted federal investments.
